title: Security Risks in AI-Generated Code
description: Understand the most common vulnerabilities introduced by AI and how to prevent them.

data.text: Why AI-Generated Code Is Not Automatically Secure

AI models are trained on vast amounts of code, including code with known vulnerabilities. They may suggest patterns that are functionally correct but introduce security weaknesses such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), hardcoded secrets, or insecure deserialization. The model optimizes for plausible-looking code, not secure code.

data.title: Watch out for these patterns:
items: XSS from unescaped user input rendered in templates
Hardcoded API keys, passwords, and tokens
Missing authentication or authorization checks on API endpoints
Path traversal from unsanitized file paths
Excessive data exposure in API responses

data.text: The OWASP Top 10 covers the most critical web application security risks. AI-generated code is particularly prone to injection flaws, broken authentication, and sensitive data exposure. When reviewing AI output, use the OWASP checklist as a mental guardrail — ask yourself whether the generated code introduces any of these risks.

rows: Missing auth checks on API routes
Explicitly request auth middleware in prompt
Returning full objects in API responses
Specify fields to return in prompt
Use template escaping; specify in prompt
Review config files generated by AI

data.text: Reviewing AI Code Like a Security Engineer

data.title: A security review checklist for AI-generated code:
items: Check all database queries for parameterization — no string concatenation
Verify all user inputs are validated and sanitized
Look for hardcoded secrets or credentials
Confirm authentication and authorization checks exist on protected routes
Verify API responses do not leak more data than necessary
Check for safe error handling — no stack traces exposed to users
Verify the AI used the correct, updated libraries (not deprecated vulnerable versions)

data.title: Treat AI code as junior developer code
data.text: The safest assumption is that AI-generated code has the security knowledge of a junior developer who has read a lot of Stack Overflow. It may know the patterns, but it does not have the experience to know which patterns are dangerous. Always run security linters and static analysis on AI-generated code before merging.

You can significantly reduce security risks by including security requirements in your prompts. Instead of asking for a generic API endpoint, ask for one with input validation, parameterized queries, authentication middleware, and rate limiting. The AI will follow these constraints and produce more secure code.

data.title: Prompting for secure code
data.content:
Instead of: "Create a login endpoint"

Try: "Create a POST /api/auth/login endpoint using Express and Prisma. Use parameterized queries (do NOT concatenate strings). Validate email and password with Zod before processing. Return 401 on invalid credentials with a generic message (do not leak whether email exists). Hash passwords with bcrypt. Add rate limiting with express-rate-limit. Return JWT on success."

data.title: Run these on AI-generated code before merging:
items: Linters (ESLint with security plugins, Bandit for Python, SpotBugs for Java)

data.title: Automate security checks in CI
data.text: Add security linters and secret scanners to your CI pipeline. This ensures every PR, including those with AI-generated code, is automatically checked for common vulnerabilities. The AI might write the code, but your CI pipeline should be the safety net.

data.title: Security with AI code
points: AI-generated code can contain vulnerabilities from training data
Always review AI code through a security lens before merging
Include security constraints directly in your prompts
Run linters, static analysis, and secret scanners automatically
Treat AI code with the same skepticism as any code review
